channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Introducing the CC Open Heritage Companion
item.description: Creative Commons: “The Creative Commons (CC) Open Heritage Companion is a practitioner’s guide developed to help cultural heritage institutions navigate the journey from closed to open collections. Grounded in the legal, policy, and ethical questions institutions face along the way, the Companion brings together 200+ curated resources, tools, and examples, organized into six chapters that guide practitioners from their first questions about openness to leading the field.”

item.title: Google is open-sourcing its 3D emoji
item.description: The Verge: “Now, if you want to, you can use Google’s 3D emoji in your own creations. The company shared some details about how it went about designing the little pictograms and why, as part of World Emoji Day on Friday.”

item.title: Hardcore IndieWeb: Run your own website 100% independently for only $0.01/day
item.description: Neatnik: “…if the idea of having complete independence and control over your content on the web is appealing to you, read on. Because that’s what Hardcore IndieWeb is all about.”

item.title: On Kalshi and Polymarket, World Cup Final Drives Bets Into the Billions
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Prediction market users are poised to make the World Cup the largest gambling event in history, analysts said. In June, total wagers on the platforms topped $50 billion for the first time, much of it driven by the soccer tournament, according to data from Dune Analytics, a crypto data tracker. That was up from about $2 billion the same month a year ago.”

item.title: Investigation reveals dozens of disguised gambling apps on the App Store in Brazil
item.description: 9to5 Mac: “A 9to5Mac investigation has uncovered more than 60 apps that behave exactly as depicted in their App Store screenshots when accessed from virtually anywhere in the world, except Brazil. When opened from a Brazilian IP address, the same apps instead reveal online betting platforms.”

item.title: What to know about the Tate brothers, social media influencers facing rape and trafficking charges
item.description: Associated Press: “Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges relate to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to ‘indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.'”

item.title: Burnham to scrap Starmer’s digital ID scheme in ‘reset of priorities’
item.description: The Guardian: “Andy Burnham is expected to scrap Keir Starmer’s plans for digital ID cards in a ‘reset of priorities’ when he enters Downing Street on Monday. The new Labour leader plans to redirect the resources earmarked for the scheme towards tackling the cost of living, his team indicated on Saturday.”

item.title: Wild animals don’t exist for your social media content
item.description: Salon: “‘Generally, if an animal is alert to your presence, you’re already too close,’ says Shervin Hess, conservation manager at Portland’s Oregon Zoo. And because humans have grown comfortable — perhaps too comfortable — around wild animals in the age of social media and smartphones, more often than not it’s the animals who wind up paying for our heedlessness.”

item.title: ChatGPT Access Tied To 9% Drop In Traditional Search
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “A recent look at U.S. desktop browsing shows ChatGPT directed people to outside websites in 5.2% of sessions, compared to 31.1% for Google searches. The paper, conducted by Bocconi University researchers, examines Comscore clickstream data to gain insight into how broader access to ChatGPT has impacted traditional search.”

item.title: 18,000 rare books, 1,000 archives in Mysuru to go digital
item.description: The Hindu: “Under this agreement, Servants of Knowledge will undertake the digitisation of approximately 18,000 rare books and 1,000 archival publications housed within the Department’s library in Mysuru. This project is dedicated to safeguarding these historical materials and making the knowledge contained within them accessible to citizens, researchers, and students across India and worldwide.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Data center opponents stage 142 protests across 42 US states
item.description: Reuters: “Opponents of the rapid buildout of data centers held ​142 protests across 42 states on Saturday in the first nationwide effort to channel anger at the AI infrastructure expansion that has ramped up over ‌the past year and roiled local politics.”

item.title: ‘A better way to be relevant’: Greens embrace data center fight
item.description: Politico: “Groups including the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, Earthjustice, and Food and Water Watch are ramping up national campaigns, activating volunteers in states and providing support for local fights against the massive artificial intelligence facilities that are spreading across the country.”

item.title: A loophole leaves Oklahoma data center water consumption largely untracked
item.description: Investigate Midwest: “While there is no official count of how many data centers are currently operating in the state, Baxtel, a data center development advisory firm, lists 55 facilities in Oklahoma. None of those facilities have applied for a water permit. Instead, they purchase water from municipal utilities, creating a gap in state oversight that leaves their water use largely untracked.”

item.title: Energy expert tells NM lawmakers Project Jupiter could roll back air quality progress by 20 years
item.description: Source NM: “Environmental advocates on Monday told New Mexico lawmakers that power plants built specifically for large data centers such as Project Jupiter could undo more than 20 years of progress on air quality.”

item.title: Will AI fix prior authorization—or make it worse?
item.description: Ars Technica: “An HHS Office of Inspector General memorandum published in 2022 pointed to more than one in 10 instances in which Medicare Advantage plans denied beneficiaries’ access to services even though they apparently met coverage rules. (Being denied access doesn’t mean patients can’t ever gain access. In 2024, for example, Medicare Advantage plans overturned 81 percent of denials upon appeal.)”

item.title: Political text messages could get more effective and annoying. Blame AI
item.description: Louisville Public Radio: “AI-powered platforms are training bots to sound like political candidates in text messages, holding personalized conversations with thousands of potential voters simultaneously. The bots are also gathering data, learning what each voter wants from their representatives and using that information to shape future campaign messaging.”

item.title: Australia demands AI companies must produce more energy than they consume, stop ‘theft’ of content
item.description: The Register: “Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has delivered a landmark speech outlining the nation’s AI policy, which will require datacenter builders to contribute more energy than they consume and mean AI companies must reach agreements with local artists and media before using their content.”

item.title: Mozilla’s Inaugural ‘State of Open Source AI’ Report Is Here
item.description: Mozilla Blog: “Today Mozilla is publishing its inaugural State of Open Source AI report, built on new analysis and a global survey of 950+ developers, showing that open models are no longer playing catch-up. The performance gap with top proprietary systems like ChatGPT and Claude has narrowed to just 3%, while costs have fallen up to 50x in three years.”

item.title: OpenAI’s first physical device is here, and it’s not what we expected
item.description: Mashable: “The device is a compact 13-key controller designed to work alongside OpenAI’s Codex coding assistant. It features a rotary dial to adjust the AI’s ‘reasoning level,’ a joystick to trigger coding workflows such as reviewing pull requests or debugging errors, programmable command keys for actions like accepting or rejecting suggestions, and RGB backlighting that changes color to reflect what an active Codex session is doing.”

item.title: Security incident disclosure — July 2026
item.description: Hugging Face: “Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system – and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.”

item.title: How The Spread Of Local AI Models Makes Copyright Enforcement Harder
item.description: Techdirt: “The EU Copyright Directive’s core assumption that the main forums for sharing material would be a few, easily controllable online giants like Google and Facebook, no longer holds. Instead, people are moving to world where millions of people are using the latest generation of open source AI tools collaboratively to generate creations. Those may or may not be based on existing copyright material, but there is no easy way to police that.”

item.title: AI Content Is Everywhere on Social Media, Especially LinkedIn
item.description: Pangram: “AI-generated content appeared across all social media platforms in our data set. The average AI rate across all scanned items was 13.8%, but specific rates varied by platform and item length. On four out of five platforms, longer content was more likely to be AI-generated than shortform content. Across all platforms, one in four longform items (25.72% of items over 250 words) were fully AI-generated.”

item.title: WVU engineers develop AI system to speed satellite tracking of wildfires
item.description: West Virginia University: “A new artificial intelligence system developed by West Virginia University engineers could help firefighters respond to wildfires sooner by enabling satellites to detect blazes and automatically adjust their positions for continued monitoring.”

item.title: Could AI be conscious?
item.description: The Guardian: “In building ever more advanced AI, we may be creating a new type of being – and this could be the most consequential thing our species has ever done. Yet we have essentially no plan for how to navigate this process ethically. That, by any reckoning, is insane. Are we creating a kind of being that matters morally? Are AI systems conscious, in some way? And, if they aren’t now, might they become so soon?” I don’t think we have to worry about that with our current “spicy autocompete” model. Good evening, Internet…

item.title: CANY Releases New Interactive Dashboard on State Prison Releases
item.description: Correctional Association of New York: “The Correctional Association of New York (CANY) today released a new interactive dashboard containing data on releases from the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS) facilities. The dashboard includes releases from January 2015 through May 2026, providing transparency into demographic profiles, commitment counties, security levels, and release types.”

item.title: WordPress 7.0.2 Release
item.description: WordPress: “The 7.0.2 security release addresses one critical and one high severity security issue. Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately. Due to the severity, the WordPress.org team have enabled forced updates via the auto-update system for sites running affected versions.”

item.title: Musk’s X, major labels end dispute over music on social-media platform
item.description: Reuters: “A group of major music publishers including Universal Music Group and Sony Music have agreed to end a legal dispute with Elon Musk’s X Corp over the use of their music on the X social-media platform, according to federal court filings.”

item.title: These Gboard Alternatives Are Open-Source and Privacy-First
item.description: Lifehacker: “Gboard is the default keyboard for Pixel smartphones and many devices that use stock Android, but it’s not the only option out there. Recently, Gboard has been swept up in a privacy controversy highlighting how your data is used by Google for its own training and collection. The data that Google collects can be intercepted and tied to individual users. Luckily, you can disable some of those data-sharing settings.”

item.title: TikTok’s plan to break into sports involves slam dunks and right hooks
item.description: Tubefilter: “As the value of sports broadcast packages continues to rise, TikTok has struck multiple deals that will bring top athletes to its platform. Upcoming broadcasts on the video app include a championship boxing match headlined by Amanda Serrano and basketball highlights courtesy of the NBA and WNBA.”

item.title: ‘Click to cancel’ rule aims to protect CT consumers from unwanted subscriptions
item.description: CT Mirror: “Under the law, which went into effect July 1, companies must notify consumers of automatic renewals and give subscribers a clear ability to cancel. If that doesn’t happen, residents can file a complaint with the state Attorney General or the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection.”

item.title: In cities across Ukraine, an exhibition featuring the sounds of the occupied Askania-Nova will be shown
item.link: In cities across Ukraine, an exhibition featuring the sounds of the occupied Askania-Nova will be shown
item.description: MOCT: “The biosphere reserve ‘Askania-Nova’ is preparing an exhibition dedicated to the sounds of the Ukrainian steppes, including the Askania steppe….The exhibitions are planned to be held in August in Kyiv and Kherson, and later the audio archive will be published on the reserve’s website.”
item.guid: In cities across Ukraine, an exhibition featuring the sounds of the occupied Askania-Nova will be shown

item.title: Bystander videos are ‘fundamentally changing how the news is made’
item.description: University of New Hampshire: “Just weeks before [Alex] Pretti’s death, Renee Good was shot and killed by federal agents during Operation Metro Surge, a large-scale ICE deployment in Minnesota. In the Good case, too, bystander videos analyzed by professional journalists contradicted the government’s account of the incident.”

item.title: Vishal Gopalan Works to Recycle 5,000 Used Tennis Balls
item.description: Bedford Citizen: “Vishal Gopalan, a rising senior at Bedford High School, is on a mission to recycle 5,000 tennis balls by the end of 2026. Having begun the project in March, Gopalan already has 1,600 balls in his collection.”

item.title: Check out thousands of photos of midcentury D.C.
item.description: The 51st: “The photos show a bygone D.C. – when there were still troughs for horses, parts of the city could be mistaken for the countryside, and Adams Morgan looked like a quaint village – and glimpses of the future, including the opening of the Whitehurst and 14th Street bridges.”

item.title: Experience the legacy of Estadio Azteca on Google Earth.
item.description: Google Blog: “Through a Google Earth and Fundación ICA collaboration, you can get an up-close look at Estadio Azteca through an interactive digital canvas and imagery dating to the 1960s. From its origins in 1961 to the clashes that crowned legends like Pelé and Maradona, the stadium has been home to six decades of sporting history that are now yours to explore.”

item.title: UNESCO Launches a Global Dialogue on the Financing of Culture
item.description: UNESCO: “How can culture become a strategic investment priority rather than a sector competing for limited resources? This question was at the heart of the first session of UNESCO’s Online Dialogue Series on Advancing the Financing of Culture, organized on 9 July 2026, with the generous support of the European Union.”

item.title: Why Immich succeeded where every other Google Photos alternative failed
item.description: How-To Geek: “It seemed like Immich came out of nowhere, but suddenly all my colleagues appear to be using it. I’m not as into self-hosting as some of them, so perhaps that’s why I’m surprised, but the more I look into it, the more obvious it seems that this photo management solution is turning into a sleeper hit. The question is: why? At first glance Immich doesn’t seem to be all that, but there’s a reason (or five) people are dropping their cloud subscriptions in favor of managing their own digital photo collections.”

item.title: This Cool Project Allows You To Emulate Old LCD Games, Including A Possible Nintendo First
item.description: Time Extension: “All of this is me arguing that LCD games did have their place in the wider gaming climate, even if today they are more commonly considered cheap plastic tat you’re more likely to find in a bargain bin than a museum. With that in mind, I was pretty happy to be sent some information recently in our news tips about a project called BrickEmuPy, a dedicated “Handheld LCD games emulator in Python with PyQt6″ that preserves a bunch of these games for future generations in a playable format.”

item.title: Introduction to KizunaShelf: A shelf for everything you love
item.description: Mudkip Mud Sport: “I settled on an Obsidian Vault where everything I care about is a Markdown file, complete with front matter and organized using Dataview and later Obsidian Bases. But manually managing a database of over 2,000 Markdown files introduced a new kind of friction: hunting down metadata, updating statuses, and tracking dates. The tedious labor of acting like a librarian replaced the actual joy of discovering what to enjoy next. KizunaShelf is the answer to all of that.”

item.title: Preserving Wales’ weightlifting stories
item.description: UK Heritage Fund: “Weightlifting Wales is safeguarding the living history of weightlifting and Para Powerlifting before it is lost. The project is recording the memories of former lifters, coaches, officials and volunteers, while digitising medals, trophies, programmes, photographs and other artefacts currently held in private collections. These materials will be preserved in a publicly accessible bilingual digital archive, supported by community exhibitions delivered through clubs across Wales.”

item.title: Lions Bay search-and-rescuers warn against dangers of Google Maps
item.description: Vancouver Sun: “Lions Bay Search and Rescue is reminding those venturing into the wilderness that Google Maps isn’t an adequate planning tool. The warning comes after hikers were rescued this week after attempting to complete the Howe Sound Crest Trail using printed Google Maps directions that said the hike would take less than half the amount of time it usually requires.”

item.title: DOJ says it’s no longer illegal to download TikTok on federal devices
item.description: CBS News: “The Justice Department determined this week a federal law banning TikTok from government devices no longer applies to the social video app.”

item.title: DraftKings sues Philadelphia to end enforcement probe following subpoena, block consumer law
item.description: Reuters: “In a complaint filed in Philadelphia federal court, DraftKings said Pennsylvania laws governing consumer protection and unfair trade practices forbade Philadelphia from enforcing a 2024 ordinance ​creating a municipal enforcement scheme to protect consumers.”

item.title: Decoy Font
item.description: Mixfont: “Decoy font is a font that prints a decoy for every letter, making it more difficult for AI to read what you type. The font works by using separate spatial frequencies to communicate two different letters in the same space.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Explore The Met in new ways with generative AI
item.description: Google Blog: “In tandem with the residency, we are also launching Art Aura, an interactive, multimodal AI experience developed by the Google Arts & Culture Lab in collaboration with The Met. Powered by Google Gemini, Art Aura allows users to drag artworks, styles or descriptive phrases into a digital zone to uncover hidden thematic connections across the centuries of art featured in The Met’s collection, creating a personalized portrait of their unique artistic taste.”

item.title: YouTube joins Meta in appealing a jury verdict that faulted them for users’ social media addiction
item.description: Associated Press: “YouTube has appealed the verdict of a landmark social media addiction lawsuit in Los Angeles, seeking to challenge the jury’s determination that the company designed its platform to hook young users without concern for their well-being.”

item.title: EU accepts action plan by Elon Musk’s X to become more transparent
item.description: Reuters: “The European Union, which fined Elon Musk’s social media ​network X €120 million ($137.2 million) last year, said on ‌Wednesday it had accepted an action plan by X to comply with transparency rules under the EU’s Digital Services ​Act.”

item.title: How to Research Private Schools Like an Investigative Reporter
item.description: ProPublica: “It can be really hard to get transparent, comprehensive information about private schools. Our investigative reporters share some suggestions for parents and guardians who want to collect it themselves.”

item.title: White House teleprompter operator made more than $100K betting on Trump’s speeches: Sources
item.description: ABC News: “President Donald Trump’s longtime teleprompter operator is believed to have made tens of thousands of dollars by placing bets on more than a dozen of Trump’s speeches on the prediction market Kalshi, federal investigators with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission found, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.”

item.title: We’re working to save the Roswell Daily Record, an American journalism institution. Here’s how.
item.description: NM.news: “The newspaper that told the world about a ‘flying saucer’ crash near Roswell in 1947 nearly became history itself this week — but just two days after announcing it would shut down, it has found a new owner and will keep publishing. The Roswell Daily Record’s ownership announced Wednesday they reached an agreement to sell to the New Mexico News Group, which will keep the paper publishing.”

item.title: Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, is investigating TikTok’s child safety measures
item.description: Engadget: “Specifically, the regulator is looking at whether TikTok has failed, or is currently failing, to comply with requirements outlined in Section 12 of the Online Safety Act 2023. This section refers to the mitigation and management of the risks of harm to children online, and how successfully they are prevented from encountering harmful content.”

item.title: MSG Suing Wired Over Article Alleging Company Kept Database Of LGBTQIA Celebrities
item.description: Stereogum: “A week ago, Wired published a report alleging Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. maintains a database of LGBTQIA celebrities. At the time, MSG said they’d be suing Wired over the article. As promised, that lawsuit was filed today.”

item.title: Archaeological and National cadastre systems join forces to protect and promote cultural heritage
item.description: Protothema: “The collaboration focuses on the further development of the Archaeological Cadastre using the geospatial foundations of the National Cadastre, the promotion and utilization of the real estate assets managed by the Ministry of Culture, and the systematic geospatial mapping of cultural heritage protection zones across the country.”

item.title: Why I Left Google DeepMind
item.description: Alex Turner: “I wanted AI ethics commitments to hold under pressure. In particular, I wanted Google DeepMind (GDM) to maintain its existing commitment against supporting killer robots. Over several months, I asked many people to act. I asked senior people⁠—respected people⁠—people with reputations silvered by their concern about AI ethics and safety. Nearly all declined.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Developers Claim OpenAI’s New AI Model is Going Rogue and Deleting Files
item.description: Gizmodo: “But one of the upshots of building highly agentic AI systems is that they’re prone to all kinds of unexpected behaviors—including now and then deleting copious amounts of files. Multiple people have reported this recently happening to them while using GPT-5.6, the newest model from OpenAI.”

item.title: Google is building a $500 million data center in rural Ohio. Neighbors are furious
item.description: Signal Cleveland: “Over 373 acres of pancake flat, former farmland, Google is building a $500 million data center here, about seven miles northwest of the county seat of Lima. The neighbors in American Township, population 14,538, are furious. They’ve stuffed public hearings and public comment boxes in a perhaps fruitless effort to block an ongoing construction project pushed by one of the most powerful companies in the world.”

item.title: Early optimism about AI data centers runs into new reality
item.description: South Jersey Climate News: “The state’s big dream of turning New Jersey into the ‘Silicon Valley’ of artificial intelligence has run smack into the reality of soaring energy costs, the unrealistic ambitions of overly optimistic lawmakers and a public backlash against the growing number of data centers.”

item.title: Operator of Mid-Atlantic power grid, which includes Maryland, to finalize key data center regulations
item.description: Baltimore Fishbowl: “The PJM Interconnection – the regional power grid operator for Maryland and 12 other states and DC – is in the midst of finalizing consequential decisions around how it will handle the electricity demand of data centers.”

item.title: Survey: Californians overwhelmingly opposed to new data centers
item.description: Cal Matters: “The latest Public Policy Institute of California poll of 1,578 adult Californians finds that 73% oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. Though the majority of both Democrats and Republicans disapprove of building data centers, Republicans are slightly more likely to favor them than Democrats.”

item.title: Mayor Mamdani Says Landlords Can’t Secretly Use AI Images to Advertise Properties
item.description: PetaPixel: “New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is having a very busy week. Just a day after announcing a ‘click-to-cancel’ rule aimed at companies like Adobe, Mamdani is cracking down on ‘deceptive landlord practices,’ including using AI-generated and AI-edited images designed to make properties look more appealing.”

item.title: White House launches cybersecurity clearinghouse to patch software flaws discovered by AI
item.description: Politico: “The Trump administration has launched a new artificial intelligence cybersecurity clearinghouse that officials say will help federal agencies, critical infrastructure owners and operators, and AI companies identify and patch software vulnerabilities discovered by advanced AI models.”

item.title: Thousands of Google workers demand layoff protections amid AI boom in petition to CEO
item.description: The Guardian: “Google workers on Thursday delivered a petition calling for layoff protections as tech giants continue to slash their workforces while pouring billions into AI.”

item.title: Lorde hits out at AI-generated Spotify feature: “We don’t want this”
item.description: NME: “With a new function, however, Spotify has been sharing the personal meaning behind songs, providing a short paragraph that explains the lyrics and how the artist has been playing it live at their shows. For Lorde, the description of her song ‘Current Affairs’ has caught her eye, and she has now hit out at it as being inaccurate and unnecessary.”

item.title: TikTok’s AI labels might not be effective, so the app is educating its users
item.description: Tubefilter: “TikTok was one of the first social media companies to add labels to AI-generated content. Those tags were first teased in 2023 and added to the app a year later. Unfortunately, AI labels don’t seem to be as effective as TikTok wants them to be.”

item.title: Linus Torvalds puts his foot down, tells anti-AI programmers to ‘fork it’
item.description: ZDNet: “Many people hate AI. They don’t trust it a bit. Linus Torvalds, creator of Linux, isn’t one of them. Torvalds thinks AI can be quite useful for programming and maintenance. Indeed, AI is explicitly approved for use in the Linux kernel.”

item.title: Researcher poisons open-weight AI model for under $100
item.description: The Register: “Katie Paxton-Fear, a lecturer in cybersecurity at Manchester Metropolitan University and staff security advocate at Semgrep, managed to install a backdoor in an open-weight AI model in about an hour for less than $100.”

item.title: Forget typosquatting; slopsquatting is the software supply chain threat created by AI coding tools
item.description: VentureBeat: “Slopsquatting is a new type of supply chain attack that uses large language model (LLM) hallucinations to inject malicious code into development workflows. The term combines ‘AI slop’ and ‘typosquatting,’ a deceptive practice where attackers register misspelled or lookalike versions of popular domains to prey on users who enter URLs incorrectly.”

item.title: Meta Oversight Board finds top AI models less likely to criticize repressive regimes
item.description: Reuters: “AI models from leading labs including Anthropic and OpenAI are much less likely to criticize governments known for restricting free speech, Meta’s Oversight Board said on Thursday.”

item.title: Tallahassee neighbor launches ItsMyScene to connect local bands, venues, and fans all in one place
item.description: WTXL: “Jacob Sanford launched ItsMyScene, a community-driven website putting local bands, venues, and shows in one place. Sanford first tried the idea in the early 2000s with TallahasseeShows.com. More than two decades later, he’s bringing it back with new technology and a bigger vision.” Early days but looks promising.

item.title: NCDOT Launches Interactive ‘Projects Near Me’ Tool
item.description: North Carolina Department of Transportation: “The N.C. Department of Transportation recently launched an interactive online tool called Projects Near Me, where people can explore a map featuring a wide range of state transportation project data. The map is searchable by address, making it easy to find projects near any location, and by project identification number in the State Transportation Improvement Program (STIP). It can also display projects by county or NCDOT Highway Division.”

item.title: YouTube clarifies that creators can’t monetize “generic or repetitive content,” content that’s “unsatisfying or off-putting,” or content with fake AI “experts”
item.description: Tubefilter: “To be clear, this is not a new policy. The update is a communications fix: clearer, more actionable language so creators know why a channel gets flagged. The rules themselves haven’t changed, and creators are not facing demonetization for new reasons.”

item.title: KnuckleBonz reveal details of a 3D digital museum in collaboration with the late Metallica bassist’s estate
item.description: Louder: “KnuckleBonz, the company which creates officially licensed statues of musical icons, has announced details of a ‘first-of-its-kind immersive 3D digital platform’ celebrating the life of the late Metallica bassist Cliff Burton.”

item.title: Trump Media to sell instant access to ‘market-moving’ social posts
item.description: BBC: “Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, is launching a paid service to give Wall Street firms high-speed access to its most influential posts. From 1 August, instant updates will be delivered from ‘the highest-ranking’ accounts, it said. US President Donald Trump currently has the most followers on the platform.”

item.title: Musk promises purge after Grok Build caught sending entire repos to the cloud
item.description: The Register: “The researcher who exposed Grok Build uploading users’ entire repositories to cloud storage says the transfers have stopped after a server-side change. Elon Musk has separately promised that all previously uploaded user data will be deleted.”

item.title: US judge blocks Trump administration’s visa limits for social media researchers
item.description: Reuters: “A federal judge on ‌Tuesday blocked U.S. ‌President Donald Trump’s administration ​from enforcing a policy that targets foreign nationals who study ‌disinformation ⁠and hate speech on social media ⁠for visa denials and deportation.”

item.title: She knew he wasn’t real. She was in love with him anyway. One woman’s story of a romance scam
item.description: Associated Press: “Romance scams are on the rise across the United States. Last year, more than 49,000 Americans reported losing a collective $1.3 billion to romance scams, according to available FTC data shared with The Associated Press. That’s an increase of at least 14% and likely more from the previous year. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 lockdowns that fractured communities and frayed the social fabric of society, there are more lonely people than ever.”

item.title: He saw a pit on Google Maps. It turned out to be a 390-million-year-old meteor crater
item.description: CBC: “Amateur astronomer Joël Lapointe stumbled upon what he thought looked like a suspicious pit in Quebec’s Côte-Nord region while he was wandering with his Google Maps cursor in 2024. He was simply trying to plan his camping vacation when he spotted something unexpected on his screen — what researchers recently confirmed is a previously unidentified, 390-million-year-old meteor crater.”

item.title: Kalshi to offer betting on drug trial results and FDA regulatory decisions
item.description: The Guardian: “Kalshi is expanding its wagers to include bets on drug trial results, an expansion into new predictions territory as platforms continue to rapidly gain popularity and offer opportunities to bet on virtually anything.”

item.title: Cambridge and Oxford join forces to unlock over a million biological records for climate research
item.description: University of Cambridge: “The University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford will lead a major new partnership to digitise over 1.1 million natural history specimens, creating a step-change in how researchers and conservationists access vital biodiversity data.”

item.title: Legendary Livermore lamp reaches 125-year milestone
item.description: Danville SanRamon: “Since 1901, the [Centennial Light Bulb] has burned for over 1.5 million hours with intermittent outs, according to retired deputy fire chief Tom Bramell of the Livermore-Pleasanton Fire Department. Besides in-person visits to its home at LPFD’s Fire Station No. 6, the bulb has grown its following with its own website, livestream camera feed, email address and social media account, not to mention its features in film, TV shows and international news.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Keeping Flickr Safe: Our Inactive Account Policy
item.description: Flickr Blog: “At Flickr, we’re committed to maintaining a platform that’s secure, trustworthy, and built for photographers who are passionate about sharing their work. As part of that ongoing commitment, we’re introducing a policy to remove inactive accounts that have never been used.”

item.title: Samsung Health won’t delete all of your data if you opt out of AI training after all [U]
item.description: 9to5 Google: “In a statement to 9to5Google, Samsung says that it won’t delete all of your data if you opt-out of AI training. Rather, it will only delete ‘data collected for AI development.’ In other words, it sounds like it is deleting data from Samsung’s end rather than the user’s.”

item.title: Disappeared by Google: Search giant wiped user reviews on ICE detention centers
item.description: San Francisco Standard: “The company has disabled reviews for almost all of the country’s immigration detention centers over the past year, according to a study by a Tulane University professor that was published in June(opens in new tab). It’s unclear when the company began disabling reviews for the more than 100 ICE detention facilities it lists in Google Maps, but by August 2025, the number with review sections was 26. Now only four have Google review scores and accompanying written reviews.”

item.title: Social Media Face-Off: What’s Keeping Plastic Surgery Influencers Up at Night
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Educated speculation made these plastic surgeons and aesthetics experts niche stars in their own right. And since they’ve infiltrated my algorithm, I’ve noticed that many are starting to use their platforms for more than analyzing actresses and posting before-and-after shots of their own clientele. Social media’s doctors are suddenly anxious to debunk the gospel of looksmaxxers.”

item.title: We received two DMCA takedown requests via Google from an entity “Jellybean” for 2012 reporting on Android Jelly Bean
item.description: Pocketables: “The two articles in question were written on October 8, 2012, and December 10, 2012, and assuming that ‘jamelizsmth’ on tik-tok is this person, which everything seems to indicate, she was 9 years old when those were published. I wasn’t the writer as a note, and they’re not about her.”

item.title: Copyright Office Will Increase Photo Registration Cost by 55% in 120 Days
item.description: PetaPixel: “The United States Copyright Office notified Congress today that it will move forward with its plan to increase group registration of photographs from $55 to $85 in 120 days, unless it intervenes.”

item.title: Greenland research centre halts new collaborations with US to protect its scientists
item.description: Euronews: “The Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the Arctic island’s leading environmental and natural-resource research centre, is halting new collaboration with US partners to protect its data and scientists.”

item.title: Women journalists – worldwide and here at home – face outsized online attacks
item.description: Poynter: “Women journalists face online attacks at a higher rate compared to their male counterparts. In 2020, almost three quarters (73%) of 901 women journalists, surveyed globally for UNESCO, had experienced online violence, characterized as threats, harassment and abuse. These attacks include racism, religious bigotry, sectarianism, ableism, homophobism and transphobism, where they intersect with misogyny and sexism.”

item.title: DOOM Runs (slowly) In A IBM PC-Compatible CSS Sheet
item.description: Hackaday: “Just when you thought we’d run out of things to port DOOM to, here comes [Ahmed Amer] with his CSS-DOS, a massive 300 MB CSS style sheet, that runs not just DOS, but Windows 1.0 and, of course, DOOM. The CSS sheet isn’t holding a DOOM port this time, though — it’s holding a full IBM PC compatible, with a simulated 8086, 640 kB of RAM, floppy and VGA controllers. Yes, in one style sheet. We did mention it was 300 MB, right?” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: I Got Slopped
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “My biography is 90 pages long and should be shorter. It combines facts about me that are widely available on the internet, such as where I grew up, with generic insights that could be true of anyone, like a horoscope spread over dozens of pages. … The book is flattering, fabricated and absolutely packed with em dashes. It bears all the signs of A.I. slop.”

item.title: Data center opposition out in force at contentious Munster meeting
item.description: The Lansing Journal: “The question of whether or not Munster will adopt proposed zoning language that would allow data centers to be built in the town generally or at the proposed Kenmara Technology Park is still up in the air. What’s not up for debate is how Munster residents feel about that possibility: They’re against it, and want Town officials to ban them outright.”

item.title: Amsterdam activists throw acid at Microsoft datacenter project
item.description: The Register: “In the United States, we usually protest datacenters peacefully – picket signs, council meeting comments, and all that – with mixed results. In the Netherlands, activists throw water balloons filled with an acidic mixture at datacenter foundations, also with questionable effectiveness.”

item.title: Data Centers Are Booming. Who Benefits?
item.description: Georgia Tech: “The researchers’ clearest finding is that metropolitan areas capture most of the economic benefits from data centers, while rural areas see far fewer spillover effects. While metro counties saw increases in employment and new business growth, non-metro counties saw no measurable gains.”

item.title: Michigan Futures Initiative to launch pilot project on sustainable AI data centers
item.description: Michigan Daily: “The Michigan Futures Initiative — a University of Michigan interdisciplinary research initiative — recently launched its pilot project, researching ways to create ethical and sustainable artificial intelligence and data centers. The project’s team hopes to announce its findings this fall.”

item.title: FBI Has Looked at Using Questionable AI Tech to Review Signatures on Seized Mail-In Ballots
item.description: ProPublica: “As part of President Trump’s continued push to discredit the results of the 2020 election, his administration has considered using AI technology to scrutinize tens of thousands of ballots seized in Fulton County, Georgia, ProPublica has learned.”

item.title: Whitmer rolls out data center plan, calls on lawmakers to pass laws protecting energy customers
item.description: Michigan Advance: “Amid criticism for her support of data center development in Michigan and opposition to a statewide moratorium, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer on Wednesday unveiled a plan intended to ensure affordable and responsible data center growth while protecting residents from higher energy costs.”

item.title: About 300 Netflix Titles Used Generative AI This Year, Company Reveals
item.description: Variety: “Roughly 300 Netflix programs across the streamer’s library have used generative AI across their production process so far this year, the company revealed in its second-quarter earnings report on Thursday.”

item.title: Microsoft’s Nadella criticizes Anthropic’s Fable for being ‘editorially controlled’
item.description: CNBC: “Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella told employees Wednesday that Anthropic’s limits on requests that users submit to the startup’s high-end Fable artificial intelligence model don’t make sense.”

item.title: Roblox announces ‘Build,’ AI tools that let anyone create games
item.description: Mashable: “Using Build, users will be able to generate environments, characters, visual styles, gameplay mechanics, sound, and more without leaving the Roblox app and without needing to know the technical elements of game development. Game-makers will be able to provide Build with conversational, natural language prompts in order to develop their games and experiences.”

item.title: Trump-Appointed Federal Judge Scolds DOJ for Including Fake AI-Generated Case in Pleading
item.description: Mediaite: “Attorneys with the Department of Justice were scolded by a federal judge in an order Thursday for using what appeared to be a fake AI-generated case citation.”

item.title: A hacker accessed Suno source code that reportedly details how the company scraped millions of songs
item.description: Engadget: “Suno — an app that vomits out soulless audio in the form of AI-generated ‘music’ — has been hacked. According to 404 Media, the hacker accessed data related to Suno’s training practices, as well as details on its customers.”

item.title: AI Slop and Evidence about Evidence: Why Philosophy Journals Should Reject AI-Written Prose
item.description: The Splintered Mind: “I don’t want to read your AI-generated email. Lots of reasons why, but here’s the core of it: I want the text to reflect your thoughts. I want to know that you, the human, actually had those ideas and had them authentically enough to express them in exactly the form I see on the page. For personal emails, I want this for personal reasons. For philosophically substantive emails, I want this for evidential reasons. Philosophy journals should also want human-generated rather than AI-generated text for the same evidential reasons.”

item.title: Google AI Mode ads reach nearly 30% of queries: Study
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google’s AI Mode showed text ads on 29.45% of commercial queries in a new SE Ranking study, less than a year after ads began appearing in AI-generated search answers. Ads appeared on 14,733 queries in the study, which analyzed U.S. commercial searches where text ads could appear, excluding product carousels.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: CLIMBS launches real-time network to forecast Kentucky landslides
item.description: University of Kentucky: “The Slope Hydrologic Monitoring Network website is a pioneering digital platform that offers real-time insights into the stability of Kentucky’s hillslopes…. The new monitoring network consists of 24 stations strategically placed across landslide-prone terrain in Eastern Kentucky. These stations act as a first-of-its-kind, near real-time slope monitoring network in the eastern U.S., measuring vital data every 15 minutes.”

item.title: A chief creative officer’s quest to document NYC soccer culture
item.description: Marketing Brew: “Some teams are quite official: Chinatown Soccer Club has played together since 2002 against clubs from around the world, while First Touch Football Club has been together since 2012, gathering at 7a.m. every weekday. ManChestHair United has an official sponsor (and a killer name).”

item.title: The next wave of emoji could help you evoke beauty and existential dread
item.description: Engadget: “Bless the Unicode Consortium for enabling humans to express themselves more freely through the universal language of emoji. Ahead of World Emoji Day on July 17 (i.e. the date shown on the calendar icon), Unicode Emoji Subcommittee-Chair Jennifer Daniel offered a peek at nine new designs that should hit your devices by next spring.”

item.title: YouTube TV is Adding More Channels
item.description: Cord Cutters News: “This week, YouTube TV has updated its main channel lineup on its website to include several networks from Allen Media Group, signaling a broader partnership that brings new entertainment, lifestyle, and specialized programming to subscribers.”

item.title: Help me update my giant list of film-photo blogs
item.description: Down the Road: “Hi everybody! Every August I post an updated list of all the film-photography blogs that I know about. It’s meant to be a service to the whole film community. This year I’d like to ask you in advance if you publish a film-photography blog, or know of one, that has escaped my notice.” Last year’s list is still available. It’s extensive!

item.title: Broadside: Cross-posting app for Bluesky & Mastodon
item.description: Cruftbox: “A broadside is when a ship fires every cannon on one side at once. That’s the whole idea: I write a post once, attach my images, add alt text, and Broadside fires it at every Bluesky and Mastodon account I’ve got in a single click.”

item.title: Meta smart glasses get pro cyclist kicked out of race
item.description: Mashable: “Professional cyclist Willie Smit went 14 years without being disqualified from a race. Then he put on a pair of smart glasses. The 33-year-old South African veteran cyclist was removed from the opening stage of the Tour of Magnificent Qinghai after officials determined that his video-recording glasses violated Union Cycliste Internationale rules governing onboard technology.”

item.title: Patchpocalypse Now: Microsoft tops last month’s record with 622 Patch Tuesday CVEs
item.description: The Register: “Remember last month when we were awed by Microsoft’s record-setting Patch Tuesday that addressed 206 CVEs? That was a quaint era compared to this month: Redmond just rolled out patches for 622 CVEs specific to its products, slightly more than tripling last month’s all-time high.”

item.title: One name at a time: How Die Zeit built a searchable database of Nazi Party members
item.description: NiemanLab: “A few weeks after the archive’s release was reported in German media, Die Zeit had built a searchable database that transformed millions of scanned membership cards into an accessible public resource. The project has since attracted millions of searches, with users uncovering the names of grandparents, great-uncles, and other relatives whose party membership had long remained hidden within the archive.”

item.title: As Dharavi is set to disappear, a digital twin will ensure it survives after it’s gone
item.description: India Today: “Dharavi is being preserved in a detailed digital twin before redevelopment starts in full swing and reshapes the settlement, which is India’s largest slum in Mumbai. The 3D archive is expected to guide relocation and planning while preserving a record of the neighbourhood that future generations will never experience.”

item.title: Santa Barbara Airport launches “Library on the Fly”
item.description: KSBY: “Santa Barbara Airport (SBA) and the Santa Barbara Public Library (SBPL) have partnered to launch Library on the Fly, a free book exchange located inside the airport terminal. The program encourages passengers to take a book to read while traveling or donate one they’ve already finished, creating an easy way to share stories with fellow travelers.” Good morning, Internet…
